title: API recovery playbook — operator scratch draft
body:
Purpose and scope
This is a working SRE operator playbook for the most common API degradations we see: persistent timeouts, burst 429s (quota + upstream backpressure), streaming stalls/lossy streams, and elevated 5xx/error rates. Focus is on fast triage, temporary mitigations to restore customer traffic, and clear escalation + follow-up actions for RCA.

Notes-to-self style: keep this compact — cheat-sheet for first 20 minutes. Longer remediation and RCA steps below.

Fast triage (first 0–10 minutes)
- Confirm scope: single route? single model? region? customer tier?
  - Dashboard: Console -> Routes -> last 15m error breakdown.
  - Quick checks: SLOs/alerts (PagerDuty) and Slack #sre-incidents.
- Verify signal sources (don’t assume one):
  - Metrics: api.requests.total, api.requests.errors, api.latency.p50/p95/p99, api.rate_limit.denied
  - Logging: search for consistent error strings (e.g., "upstream timeout", "KV cache miss storm", "exceeded tokens")
- Immediate public comms: if customers are impacted and PD paged, post a short status note in #customer-incidents and add to status.redwood.io if needed.

Quick diagnostic queries (examples)
- PromQL: 5m rate of 5xx by route
  - sum(rate(api_response_count{status=~"5..",route=~".*"}[5m])) by (route)
- PromQL: 429 spikes by model/route
  - sum(rate(api_response_count{status="429"}[5m])) by (route, model)
- Log filter: look for repeated client IPs or same request fingerprint -> may indicate retry storms
  - logs: "error" AND "upstream" AND route:

Initial mitigation tactics (choose based on cause)
- Localized throttling and traffic shaping
  - If a single route is spiking 429s downstream but causing systemic load, set temporary stricter per-key rate limits for tier=free or apply short-term token bucket limits.
  - Example: push a temporary rate-limit policy via config-api: curl -X POST $CONFIG_API/policies -d '{"route":"/v1/generate","limit":30,"burst":60,"scope":"tier:free"}'
- Fallback routing to cheaper/less-loaded model variant
  - If model A is overloaded, shift a small percentage of traffic to model A-quantized or an earlier version with same interface. Use rollout policy in Console -> Rollouts -> create canary 10% traffic to model-B.
- Shorten max tokens and sequence lengths for affected route (makes tokens cheaper and faster)
  - Config change: response.max_tokens = 256 (temporary)
- Disable expensive features in-flight (embedding + generation combos, heavy tool-calls) for impacted customers via feature-flag gateway.

Streaming-specific quick fixes
- If streaming is stalled/partial payloads:
  - Check edge gateways (nginx/Envoy) for long-lived connections and RST rates.
  - If many partial streams, enable adaptive chunking: reduce chunk size and increase flush frequency in the streamer config.
  - If KV cache pressure causing stalls, temporarily disable prefix caching for long-tail customers causing cache churn.

Timeouts root causes & mitigations
- Common causes: slow upstream model (GPU contention / OOM / quantized fallback), overloaded inference queue, network glibches between region edge and serving plane.
- Fast mitigations:
  - Increase concurrency on tolerant dedicated pools, or briefly scale a burst pool (if Dedicated)
  - Promote a lower-latency model variant as a fallback for the affected route
  - If due to a single node: cordon + restart node (kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets) and let autoscaler replace it — but only if we see node-level OOMs or driver failures.
  - For transient network blips, shift the route to another region if cross-region fallback is enabled.

429s (rate-limit) diagnostics and play
- Distinguish types: external client-side retries vs internal backpressure returning 429.
  - Client retry storms: identify top client keys in the 429s logs and apply short-term key-level adjustments (apply a 5s jittered retry-after).
  - Internal backpressure: our proxy returns 429 when queue length > threshold. Look at queue_length metric and worker_utilization.
- Mitigations:
  - Increase proxy queue capacity cautiously. This reduces 429 but may increase latency; prefer to widen capacity only for short windows.
  - Temporarily reduce concurrency per model to keep tail latency reasonable.

Elevated 5xx rates
- Common culprits: client input causing unhandled exceptions, model runtime crashes, dependency outages (KV store / vector DB), or config bugs.
- Steps:
  - Scan logs for stack traces or repeating error tokens.
  - If exception from a single microservice, restart only that deployment (kubectl rollout restart deploy/<svc>) and monitor.
  - If dependency (e.g., vector DB) is failing, follow that system’s runbook and enable cached fallbacks.

Escalation ladder (who to call)
- Primary SRE oncall -> escalate to serving-runtime lead if model runtime suspected.
- If infrastructure (GPU host or cloud region) suspected -> ping infra-oncall + cloud provider support.
- If customer-impacting SLA breach and legal/comms needed -> page Escalations pager (Ops/Support lead).

Post-restoration checklist (first 24 hours)
- Keep traffic at reduced rate for 60–120 minutes after mitigation before ramping to normal. Note exact timestamps and config changes in incident Jira.
- Snapshot metrics (pre/mitigation/post) and save to Confluence incident page.
- Collect sample failing requests with headers + payloads (strip PII).
- If a node/container was restarted, collect core dumps, driver logs, and GPU metrics.

RCA and follow-ups (deferred work)
- Root-cause categories to consider: autoscaler tuning, model/kernel regression, cache churn, client retry behaviour, bad release, infra flakiness.
- Required remedials (pick at least one actionable):
  - Add a per-route canary for next deploy (fail-fast if latency increases > 15% on canary).
  - Harden proxy to return Retry-After header and sample request IDs on 429s for tracing.
  - Add client-side guidance to SDK: exponential backoff + jitter + capped retries, and default shorter max_tokens for free tier.
  - Revisit autoscaler thresholds (queue growth vs CPU/GPU utilization) and add a conservative burst target.

Operational experiments to run post-incident
- A/B test quantized fallback vs dynamic batching for 2 weeks to measure p95 improvement and cost delta.
- Run synthesized retry storm on staging (with rate-limited clients) to validate 429 behaviour and backoff guidance.

Open questions / TODOs
- Do we have telemetry to map a 429 to the precise queue owner (service instance + queue id)? If not, add it.
- Should streaming have a separate, lower-priority queue to avoid head-of-line blocking? (Experiment proposal)
- Decide default max_tokens for free tier (proposal: 256) and publish SDK update.

Operator quick commands (copyable)
- Check p95 latency by route (PromQL):
  - histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(api_request_duration_seconds_bucket{route=~"/v1/.*"}[5m])) by (le, route))
- Roll back a model rollout:
  - curl -X POST $CONSOLE_API/rollouts/rollback -d '{"route":"/v1/generate","target":"previous"}'
- Restart a single deployment:
  - kubectl -n production rollout restart deployment/serving-runtime-worker-12

Incident metadata to capture (always add to incident ticket)
- Time window of impact, affected routes, affected models, customer lists, mitigation steps, config changes (with timestamps), and follow-ups with owners and due dates.

Appendix: quick heuristics for deciding mitigation
- If latency spike with low error rate -> suspect batching or kernel slowdown; favor scaling workers or switching kernels.
- If 429s concentrated on low-tier keys -> apply key-level throttling and customer communication.
- If streaming partial payloads but not errors -> check edge timeouts and connection health; do not restart model nodes immediately.

Notes for doc hygiene
- This is intentionally terse. Convert to a formal runbook page after 2 incidents of the same class with the suggested postmortem attached.
- Action items assigned during an incident should be converted to Jira tickets labeled SRE-ops within 2 business days.

Signed-off-by: Lina Patel (SRE) — operator scratch; please add your post-incident notes inline here and link the final RCA.
